thread.title_full: Orange County program gives first-time youth offenders alternative to court system - NewsBreak

author: Cindy Bae
title: Orange County program gives first-time youth offenders alternative to court system - NewsBreak
text:
By Cindy Bae ,
5 hours ago
Orange County's Youth Deflection Program is providing young people who are first-time offenders with an alternative to entering the court system, county officials say.
The program launched in 2021 and has served more than 150 young people, according to Youth Deflection Program coordinator Tami Pfeifer.
"Even though it's still a juvenile system, it can still have negative effects on their record, or their future education," Pfeifer said. "We wanted to have an off-ramp to that because we know that young people make mistakes."
County data shows delinquency complaints increased 143% over a five-year period. During the 2021-22 period, the county recorded 316 complaints involving 103 young people. According to the data, 38% of complaints were classified as minor offenses and 39% as serious offenses. The data does not provide details about the specific offenses.
Pfeifer said the program is designed to prevent young people from becoming more deeply involved in the legal system.
"Once kids get involved in the in the legal system, it can snowball and they have a much higher rate of recidivism and getting into deeper trouble," Pfeifer said.
She said the program seeks to hold participants accountable while addressing factors that may contribute to their behavior. Individualized plans can include school-based therapy, peer mentoring and family counseling.
"Kids don't want to be in trouble," Pfeifer said. "They want to have success. So, this is an opportunity to stack them up when they are having difficulties, so that they can be successful in the future."
The Chapel Hill Police Department is among the program's community partners, and officers can refer eligible young people to the program. Pfeifer said those partnerships will be important to expanding the program's reach and helping more young people move forward.
"I know most of these kids are wanting to do their best," Pfeifer said. "They want to be connected positively to school, to community, and giving them these resources and support. I know they're more likely to be held, cared for, and move positively towards the direction they want."
